q: Under AU-C 570 for a nonissuer reporting under U.S. GAAP, over what period does the auditor evaluate whether substantial doubt exists about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern?
choices: One year after the date the financial statements are issued or available to be issued
One year after the balance sheet date
A reasonable period not to exceed one year beyond the balance sheet date
Eighteen months after the report date
exp: When the applicable framework is U.S. GAAP (ASC 205-40), the look-forward period is one year after the financial statements are issued or available to be issued, and AU-C 570 aligns with the framework's period. A period of a reasonable time not exceeding one year beyond the balance sheet date is the PCAOB AS 2415 period.

q: An auditor identifies conditions raising substantial doubt but concludes management's plans alleviate that doubt. Management adequately discloses the conditions and plans. Under AU-C 570, the auditor's report on the nonissuer should:
choices: Include a separate section titled 'Substantial Doubt About the Entity's Ability to Continue as a Going Concern'
Not be required to include a going concern section, although the auditor may include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
Include a qualified opinion
Include an adverse opinion
exp: When substantial doubt is alleviated by management's plans, AU-C 570 requires evaluating the adequacy of disclosure but does not require a going concern section; an emphasis-of-matter paragraph is optional. The separate section is required only when substantial doubt remains.

q: Which of the following conditions, considered alone, would most likely raise substantial doubt about an entity's ability to continue as a going concern?
choices: A significant increase in the allowance for credit losses due to a new accounting standard
The entity's decision to discontinue a profitable product line to focus on another
Default on a loan agreement, with the lender having the right to accelerate the debt, and denial of credit by key suppliers
The resignation of the entity's controller
exp: Loan default with acceleration rights and loss of trade credit are classic indicators of liquidity problems listed in AU-C 570. An accounting change, a strategic product decision, or a controller's resignation do not by themselves indicate inability to meet obligations.

q: When evaluating management's plans to mitigate going concern conditions, the auditor primarily considers whether:
choices: The plans have been approved by the entity's lenders
The plans were prepared by an outside consultant
The plans eliminate all losses in the next year
It is probable that the plans will be effectively implemented and, if so, that they will mitigate the conditions
exp: AU-C 570 and ASC 205-40 require evaluating whether it is probable that management's plans will be effectively implemented and will mitigate the relevant conditions. Lender approval or consultant preparation may be evidence but are not the standard, and eliminating all losses is not required.

q: Management's plan to alleviate substantial doubt depends on continued financial support from the entity's majority owner. Which evidence is most important for the auditor to obtain?
choices: Evidence of the owner's intent and ability to provide the support, such as a written agreement and the owner's financial capacity
An oral statement from the CFO that the owner has always provided support
The owner's résumé
A projection showing the entity will be profitable without support
exp: AU-C 570 indicates that when plans rely on support from third parties or owners, the auditor evaluates their intent and ability, often through written evidence and the supporter's financial capacity. An oral representation from management is insufficient on its own.

q: An auditor concludes that substantial doubt exists and management's disclosure of the matter is inadequate. The effect is material but not pervasive. The auditor should express:
choices: An unmodified opinion with a going concern section
A qualified opinion
A disclaimer of opinion
An unmodified opinion with an other-matter paragraph
exp: Under AU-C 570 and AU-C 705, inadequate going concern disclosure is a misstatement resulting in a qualified or adverse opinion depending on pervasiveness. A going concern section accompanies an unmodified opinion only when disclosure is adequate.

q: Management of a nonissuer prepared financial statements on the going concern basis, but the auditor concludes liquidation is imminent and the going concern basis is inappropriate. The auditor should:
choices: Issue an unmodified opinion with a going concern section
Issue a qualified opinion
Express an adverse opinion
Issue a disclaimer of opinion
exp: AU-C 570 requires an adverse opinion when the financial statements are prepared using the going concern basis but, in the auditor's judgment, that basis is inappropriate. A going concern section is used when the basis is appropriate but substantial doubt exists.

q: A nonissuer appropriately adopts the liquidation basis of accounting because liquidation is imminent. How should the auditor report, assuming the statements are fairly presented on that basis?
choices: Adverse opinion because the going concern basis was not used
Disclaimer because the future is uncertain
Qualified opinion
Unmodified opinion, and the auditor may include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph about the liquidation basis
exp: When the liquidation basis is appropriate and properly applied, the opinion is unmodified, and an emphasis-of-matter paragraph is generally appropriate to draw attention to the basis. Adverse opinions are reserved for inappropriate use of the going concern basis.

q: Which statement is accurate about wording in the going concern section of an auditor's report under AU-C 570?
choices: The report must use the terms 'substantial doubt' and 'going concern' and must not use conditional language about the conclusion
The report may state 'if the company continues to suffer losses, there may be substantial doubt'
The report should state the probability that the entity will fail
The report must name the lenders whose actions caused the doubt
exp: AU-C 570 requires the terms 'substantial doubt' and 'going concern' and prohibits conditional language that expresses the conclusion tentatively. The report does not quantify probability of failure or name specific lenders.

q: Management refuses to perform an evaluation of the entity's ability to continue as a going concern as required by the applicable framework. The auditor should:
choices: Perform the evaluation on management's behalf and issue an unmodified opinion
Consider the implications for the auditor's report, as this may constitute a scope limitation or misstatement
Ignore the refusal because the auditor makes its own evaluation
Report the refusal to the state board of accountancy
exp: AU-C 570 indicates that management's unwillingness to make or extend its evaluation may have implications for the report, such as a scope limitation. The auditor's own evaluation does not substitute for management's required assessment.

q: When events or conditions raising substantial doubt are identified, which of the following is a required additional procedure under AU-C 570?
choices: Confirming all receivables with customers
Obtaining a legal letter from every vendor
Requesting written representations from management regarding its plans and their feasibility
Reperforming the prior-year audit
exp: AU-C 570 requires additional procedures including evaluating management's plans and requesting written representations about the plans and the probability of their implementation. The other procedures are not specifically required.

q: Management's plans rely on a cash flow forecast projecting significant sales growth. Which procedure is most appropriate?
choices: Accept the forecast because management is responsible for it
Recompute only the mathematical accuracy of the forecast
Compare the forecast to the budget prepared by the same people
Evaluate the reliability of the underlying data and whether there is adequate support for the significant assumptions
exp: When prospective financial information is significant to management's plans, AU-C 570 requires evaluating the reliability of the underlying data and support for significant assumptions. Mathematical accuracy alone does not address whether the projected growth is reasonable.

q: In an issuer audit under PCAOB AS 2415, the period the auditor considers when evaluating going concern is:
choices: A reasonable period of time, not to exceed one year beyond the date of the financial statements being audited
One year after the date the financial statements are issued
Two years beyond the balance sheet date
The operating cycle of the entity
exp: AS 2415 uses a reasonable period not exceeding one year beyond the date of the financial statements being audited. The 'issued or available to be issued' period derives from U.S. GAAP and AU-C 570; the auditor must still consider the framework's disclosure requirements.

q: A nonissuer's prior-year audit report included a going concern section. In the current year, substantial doubt no longer exists. The current comparative report should:
choices: Repeat the prior-year going concern section
Not repeat the going concern section
Include an adverse opinion on the prior year
Include a qualified opinion on the current year
exp: If substantial doubt existed in the prior period but has been removed in the current period, AU-C 570 indicates that the going concern section included in the prior report should not be repeated. No modification is needed for either year.

q: Which of the following is required to be communicated to those charged with governance under AU-C 570 when the auditor identifies events or conditions raising substantial doubt?
choices: The auditor's fee for the additional work
The names of the employees who prepared the cash flow forecast
Whether the events or conditions constitute substantial doubt, the effect on the report, and the adequacy of related disclosures
Only the matters that were not resolved by year-end
exp: AU-C 570 requires communicating whether events or conditions constitute substantial doubt, whether management's plans alleviate it, the adequacy of disclosures, and the implications for the report. Fees and specific employee names are not part of this communication.

q: The absence of reference to substantial doubt in an auditor's report should be viewed as:
choices: A guarantee that the entity will continue as a going concern for one year
Evidence that management's plans are probable of implementation
A conclusion that no conditions exist that require disclosure
Not a guarantee of the entity's ability to continue as a going concern
exp: AU-C 570 states the auditor cannot predict future events, so the absence of a going concern reference does not guarantee continuation. The auditor's evaluation is based on information available at the report date.

q: A nonissuer's financial statements are being audited, and the auditor is concerned about going concern but management has not yet approved the financial statements several months after year-end. How might this delay affect the evaluation?
choices: The auditor should consider the reasons for the delay, which may relate to going concern, and evaluate events through the later date
The delay has no effect because the look-forward period is fixed from the balance sheet date
The auditor should date the report as of the balance sheet date
The delay requires an adverse opinion
exp: AU-C 570 notes that a significant delay in approval may relate to going concern issues and requires the auditor to inquire into the reasons; because the GAAP period runs from the issuance date, the look-forward window also shifts. The report cannot be dated before the auditor obtains sufficient evidence.

q: Which of the following management plans would the auditor most likely view as least effective in mitigating substantial doubt?
choices: A signed commitment from a bank to refinance debt maturing within the year
A plan to sell specialized equipment that is pledged as collateral and restricted from sale under a loan covenant
A plan to sell nonessential assets for which a binding sales agreement exists
A plan to reduce discretionary expenditures that management controls
exp: AU-C 570 directs the auditor to consider restrictions on disposal of assets, such as covenants and liens, when evaluating plans to sell assets; a restricted, pledged asset sale is unlikely to be effectively implemented. Committed financing, binding sale agreements, and controllable cost reductions are more likely to mitigate the conditions.

q: An auditor's going concern evaluation identifies that the entity has a recurring negative operating cash flow but has just closed a new equity raise sufficient to fund operations for 18 months. Management discloses the conditions and the raise. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
choices: Substantial doubt exists and cannot be alleviated by an equity raise
An adverse opinion is required
Substantial doubt is alleviated, and the auditor evaluates whether disclosures are adequate
The auditor must disclaim because the future is uncertain
exp: Completed financing that funds operations beyond the look-forward period is strong evidence alleviating substantial doubt, though disclosure of the conditions and plans is still evaluated under ASC 205-40 and AU-C 570. Uncertainty about the future alone is not a reason to disclaim.

q: Which of the following is an example of an event or condition that, under AU-C 570, relates to operating matters rather than financial matters?
choices: Negative working capital
Inability to pay creditors on due dates
Arrears in dividends
Loss of a major market, key customers, or principal suppliers
exp: AU-C 570 lists loss of key markets, customers, or suppliers among operating indicators. Negative working capital, inability to pay creditors, and dividend arrears are financial indicators.

q: An auditor's evaluation of going concern under AU-C 570 is primarily based on:
choices: Audit procedures performed throughout the audit, considered in the aggregate, plus additional procedures when conditions are identified
A separate set of procedures designed solely to detect going concern issues
The client's credit rating alone
Inquiry of the entity's legal counsel
exp: AU-C 570 indicates that the auditor considers whether conditions exist based on procedures performed in planning, gathering evidence, and completing the audit, and performs additional procedures when conditions are identified. No separate set of procedures solely for going concern is required at the outset.

q: A nonissuer auditor concludes substantial doubt exists and disclosures are adequate, but management refuses to provide the requested written representations regarding its plans. The auditor should most likely:
choices: Issue an unmodified opinion with a going concern section, ignoring the refusal
Consider the refusal a scope limitation and evaluate the effect on the opinion, which may lead to a disclaimer
Issue an adverse opinion because of the misstatement
Withdraw immediately without considering the report
exp: Failure to provide required written representations is a scope limitation under AU-C 580, and AU-C 570 requires the auditor to consider its effect, which can result in a disclaimer. An adverse opinion addresses misstatements, not missing evidence.

q: Under PCAOB AS 2415, when the auditor concludes there is substantial doubt about an issuer's ability to continue as a going concern, the auditor's report should include:
choices: A qualified opinion
A key audit matter section
An explanatory paragraph that includes the phrase 'substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern'
An adverse opinion
exp: AS 2415 requires an explanatory paragraph using that phrase when substantial doubt remains, and the opinion is unmodified if disclosure is adequate. Key audit matters are an AU-C 701 concept, and a qualified opinion would arise only from inadequate disclosure.

q: Which statement about the auditor's responsibility for going concern in an audit of a nonissuer is most accurate?
choices: The auditor has no responsibility if management's evaluation concludes there is no substantial doubt
The auditor's responsibility is limited to reviewing management's disclosures
The auditor is responsible for predicting whether the entity will fail
The auditor is responsible for obtaining sufficient appropriate evidence about, and concluding on, management's use of the going concern basis and whether substantial doubt exists
exp: AU-C 570 makes the auditor responsible for evaluating management's use of the going concern basis and concluding whether substantial doubt exists, even when management concludes no doubt exists. The auditor does not predict future events.

q: An auditor determines during an audit that an entity's major lender has waived a covenant violation only through 30 days after year-end, and the debt would otherwise be callable. Which effect is most likely?
choices: The short waiver is a condition the auditor considers in the going concern evaluation and may affect classification of the debt
The waiver eliminates any going concern concern
The auditor must issue an adverse opinion
The waiver is irrelevant because it was granted after year-end
exp: A short-term waiver leaves the debt callable within the look-forward period, which is relevant to both going concern and debt classification. Information after year-end is relevant to the evaluation, so it cannot be ignored.

q: Which of the following best describes when the auditor considers management's plans under AU-C 570?
choices: Before identifying any conditions, as part of engagement acceptance
Only after concluding that events or conditions, considered in the aggregate, raise substantial doubt before consideration of management's plans
Only if the client is an issuer
Only after the auditor's report has been issued
exp: ASC 205-40 and AU-C 570 use a two-step approach: first determine whether conditions raise substantial doubt, then evaluate whether management's plans alleviate it. Plans are not evaluated before conditions are identified.

q: An auditor concludes that substantial doubt exists. The auditor also determines that the matter is so significant that the effects of multiple uncertainties on the financial statements cannot be evaluated. Under AU-C 570, the auditor may:
choices: Issue an adverse opinion
Issue a qualified opinion
In rare circumstances involving multiple uncertainties, consider expressing a disclaimer of opinion
Omit the going concern section
exp: AU-C 570 indicates that in rare cases involving multiple material uncertainties significant to the financial statements, the auditor may disclaim rather than include a going concern section. An adverse opinion is not appropriate for uncertainties that are adequately disclosed.

q: An auditor of a nonissuer included a going concern section in the auditor's report. Which statement about the auditor's opinion is accurate?
choices: The opinion is qualified for the uncertainty
The opinion is adverse
The section replaces the Basis for Opinion section
The opinion is not modified with respect to the matter, assuming adequate disclosure
exp: When disclosure is adequate, the going concern section accompanies an unmodified opinion and states the opinion is not modified with respect to the matter (AU-C 570). It is presented in addition to, not in place of, the Basis for Opinion section.

q: Under AU-C 570, which of the following must the auditor evaluate even when the auditor concludes that no substantial doubt exists?
choices: Whether the applicable financial reporting framework requires disclosures about events or conditions identified, and whether those disclosures are adequate
Whether the entity has obtained a going concern insurance policy
Whether a going concern section must nonetheless be included in the report
Whether management's plans have been approved by the lenders
exp: Even when substantial doubt is not identified, or is alleviated, the auditor considers the framework's disclosure requirements about relevant conditions (AU-C 570). No going concern section is required when there is no substantial doubt.

q: Which of the following procedures is most likely to identify conditions that indicate substantial doubt about going concern?
choices: Tests of controls over payroll authorization
Review of compliance with the terms of debt and loan agreements
Observation of the physical inventory count
Recomputation of depreciation expense
exp: AU-C 570 lists reviewing compliance with debt and loan agreements among procedures that may identify going concern conditions, such as covenant violations that permit acceleration. Payroll controls, inventory counts, and depreciation recalculation are rarely informative about liquidity.
